documents: Takahashi & Minami 2022, Limnology and Oceanography: Methods 20, 605-617 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: However, the influence on 14C analysis by BAC addition to water sample has not been assessed.

steps.action: Reviewed preservation methods (HgCl2, refrigeration, filtration, acid extraction, metal additives) and prior studies showing BAC preserves DIC and d13C in freshwater (Table 1).
steps.quote: have shown that BAC works well for DIC analysis of freshwater and seems [...] )

steps.action: Posed three aims: does BAC inhibit microbial 14C change in DIC, does the effect depend on water chemistry, and how much carbon contamination BAC adds.
steps.quote: Thus, the present study aims to determine whether BAC [...] .

steps.action: Designed initial, BAC-free and BAC-added treatments of eight natural waters, boosting microbes with beet sugar and lowering 14C with 14C-dead NaHCO3; microbe-free artificial waters isolate BAC's own effect.
steps.quote: To stimulate microbial activity and allow detection of even the slightest DIC changes that may have occurred via biological influences, beet sugar powder was added

steps.action: Set laboratory conditions: 1 mL of 1% BAC per 100 mL, PAN gas-barrier bottles, room temperature, about 2- and 4-week preservation, and 7-day glass vials for the sugar-dose series.
steps.quote: As reported by Takahashi et al. (2019a), 1 mL of 1% BAC solution per 100 mL of water sample was added unless otherwise indicated.

steps.action: Extracted CO2 with the authors' ReCEIT procedure, graphitized it and measured 14C by AMS at Nagoya; measured BAC and beet sugar isotopes by combustion, AMS and IRMS.
steps.quote: the ReCEIT procedure (Takahashi et al. 2021) was used

steps.action: Measured 14C of unboosted seawaters SW01 and SW02: initial, BAC-free and BAC-added samples were identical, which the authors note is uninformative about BAC.
steps.quote: they were identical within respective samples (Fig. 1)

steps.action: In sugar-boosted natural waters, BAC-free 14C and DIC rose strongly over about 15 and 30 days; BAC-added 14C stayed nearly constant except in seawater SW03.
steps.quote: For BAC-free water, the 14C concentrations exhibited large, nearly proportional increases over the preservation periods (Fig. 2).

steps.action: Defined and estimated the boost effect (BE) of sugar addition from 7-day DIC changes (Eq. 1) and from d13C isotopic mass balance (Eq. 4); averaged BE was 3.0-7.3.
steps.quote: the boost effect (BE) is defined as an index of how many times the DIC change in the sugar-added sample (boosted) is greater

steps.action: Checked BE by two calculation methods and across six sugar doses; the methods agreed and the dose had no significant effect.
steps.quote: there was no significant difference between the results of the two calculation methods

steps.action: Measured 14C of six microbe-free artificial waters (W09-W14, 0.6-94 pMC) as initial, BAC-free and BAC-added samples after 30-36 days.
steps.quote: All the artificial water results (W09–W14) showed identical 14C concentrations within the error ranges of AMS

steps.action: Used the unchanged BAC-free artificial waters as a control for the storage bottles' tightness.
steps.quote: No 14C changes in the BAC-free water after preservation indicate that the samples were stored well.

steps.action: Measured 14C (60.7 pMC) and d13C (-29.7 permil) of the carbon of BAC itself.
steps.quote: The 14C concentration and δ13C for the carbon of BAC itself, not the carbon dissolved in the BAC solution

steps.action: Inferred biogenic DIC (DICorg) and boost-free 14C (14Cini+org) by 14C mass balance using BE, assuming 14Corg = 100 pMC (Table 4).
steps.quote: DIC and 14C concentrations which eliminated the BE by sugar addition (DICorg and 14Cini+org) are listed in Table 4.

steps.action: Compared BAC-added with BAC-free boost-corrected changes: no change with BAC in freshwater; small but non-negligible changes in seawater SW03.
steps.quote: The DICorg and 14Cini+org of BAC-added water, except for SW03, did not change during preservation.

steps.action: Kept the claim that BAC inhibits microbial DIC and 14C change, with lower effectiveness in seawater, consistent with Gloël et al. (2015) and Takahashi et al. (2019a).
steps.quote: adding BAC is an effective treatment to obtain DIC data as it inhibits microbial activities, although it is slightly less [...]

steps.action: Proposed two rivals for the seawater shortfall: DIC from germinating spores, or loss of BAC's bactericidal effect over time.
steps.quote: This suggests two possibilities: the effects of DIC produced when the spores germinate and the inability of BAC to maintain its effects for long periods.

steps.action: Judged the short-lived-BAC rival unlikely, using Gloël et al.'s result that varying the BAC dose had no effect, while leaving it to be verified.
steps.quote: [...] seems unlikely since the experiments by Gloël et al. (2015) showed no effect

steps.action: Computed the expected 14C shift from atmospheric-CO2 blank carbon in BAC solution as a function of sample DIC, sample 14C and the number of repeated bottle uses (Fig. 5).
steps.quote: Using the reported DIC concentration of BAC solution, 14C changes in water samples owing to carbon contamination derived from BAC absorbed atmospheric CO2 were estimated

steps.action: Compared the predicted shifts with the expected AMS error and with the artificial-water results (no detectable effect even below 1 pMC); DIC concentration is the more influential parameter.
steps.quote: [...] can determine whether the 14C change is detectable by comparison with the expected error in 14C analysis by AMS.

steps.action: Concluded that BAC addition is appropriate if users watch low-DIC and low-14C samples and limit the number of times a BAC bottle is opened.
steps.quote: We, therefore, conclude that the addition of BAC to water samples is appropriate so long as the user is aware of the effects

steps.action: Calculated the carbon that full BAC decomposition would add, and the microbial carbon in freshwater from Berninger et al. (1991) abundances, to bound contamination.
steps.quote: Using the worldwide abundances and cell carbon contents of heterotrophic nanoplankton and picoplankton

steps.action: Excluded BAC decomposition and BAC-induced decomposition of microorganisms as meaningful 14C contamination sources, also citing the artificial-water results.
steps.quote: Taken together, we can conclude that the direct contribution of BAC to 14C analysis is small and need not be considered.

steps.action: Summarized: BAC is effective for groundwater, lake and river water; it is less effective in seawater; DIC monitoring matters more than 14C for blank effects.
steps.quote: showed effectiveness for freshwater samples such as groundwater, lake water, and river water

steps.action: Proposed combining BAC with filtration to remove spores in seawater, as future work.
steps.quote: Therefore, treatment with a combination of BAC and filtration can inhibit microbial influence on DIC changes

tree.answer: Microbial alteration of DIC and 14C during sample storage, and whether BAC suppresses it without adding carbon
Partly: 14C and DIC measured directly; the biogenic part inferred by mass balance correcting for the sugar boost
Characterize BAC as a non-metal disinfectant for 14C-DIC analysis
Contamination sources (blank CO2, BAC decomposition, microbe lysis); spores versus short-lived BAC for the seawater shortfall
BAC decomposition would pull 14C toward 60.7 pMC; blank CO2 shifts scale with 1/DIC and with repeated uses
Set in the laboratory: paired BAC-free and BAC-added bottles, sugar boost, 14C-dead NaHCO3, microbe-free artificial waters
Holds across freshwater types, sugar doses and two BE calculation methods; weaker in seawater
BAC effective for freshwater, slightly less for seawater; contamination negligible except low-DIC samples with a repeatedly opened bottle

end.claim: BAC is an effective inhibitor of biological DIC and 14C changes for 14C analysis of freshwater samples; it is slightly less effective in seawater, and its carbon contamination is negligible if bottle reuse is controlled for low-DIC samples.

decisive_move.sentence: The paired comparison of BAC-added and BAC-free sugar-boosted, 14C-depleted natural waters, corrected for the boost effect, is what shows that BAC suppresses biogenic 14C change in freshwater but not fully in seawater.

gates.evidence: The aims (inhibition, dependence on water chemistry, contamination) directed a controlled paired design (BAC-free versus BAC-added, sugar boost, microbe-free artificial waters), but no formal hypothesis was stated. BAC-added samples could have changed, and in seawater they did. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data: the AMS-error detectability criterion and the handling of negative DICorg are applied post hoc.

imports.item: Benzalkonium chloride as a quaternary-ammonium disinfectant
Sugar substrate addition to stimulate microbial activity (boost effect)

novelty_claims.quote: However, the influence on 14C analysis by BAC addition to water sample has not been assessed.
[...] study, the boost effect (BE) is defined as an index

limits: No peer-review file was supplied, although the acknowledgments thank two reviewers and an associate editor; changes made in review cannot be coded. One PAN bottle each was used for BAC-free and BAC-added waters, with no replicate bottles; replication is only across water types. The BE was estimated in separate 7-day glass-vial experiments, run about 90 days after collection and without BAC, then applied to the 2- and 4-week PAN experiments; the transfer is an assumption (inference). The 14Corg value is assumed to be 100 pMC. Preservation lasted at most about 30-36 days, so longer-term effectiveness is untested. The '20-40%' figure is ambiguous: the abstract says seawater changes with BAC were '20–40% lower', and the conclusions say BAC reduces changes 'by 20–40%', yet Table 4 values (0.4 vs 2.0 and 1.6 vs 3.9 mg/L) imply BAC-treated changes were about 20-40% of untreated, a reduction of 60-80% (inference). The unboosted seawaters SW01 and SW02 are acknowledged as uninformative. Sub-claims at other statuses: negligible contamination from BAC decomposition and microbe lysis is best_explanation (calculation plus artificial-water null result); the blank-contamination guidance (Fig. 5) is estimate_with_resolution from simulation; the spore explanation for the seawater shortfall is untested (none). Composition is none_fits: this is a controlled laboratory characterization of a sample-preservation method, set conditions with paired controls, not a capability-first exploration or a strong-inference test among rivals.

disagreements.target: HgCl2 and metal-additive preservation as the standard (WOCE, GLODAP, GEOTRACES practice) applied to freshwater
disagreements.support: Cites toxicity and reported alkalinity, d13C and speciation artifacts from mercury and copper in freshwater, and offers BAC as tested here.
disagreements.quote: Therefore, metal additives should be avoided when analyzing freshwater samples.

disagreements.target: Takahashi et al. (2019a): BAC effective for 10–15 days for d13C in saline waters
disagreements.support: 14C measurements show slight seawater DIC changes even within 2 weeks, attributed to the larger 14C than d13C contrast between biogenic and seawater DIC.
disagreements.quote: Meanwhile, the results of the present study show slight DIC changes even during short-term preservation

disagreements.target: Gloël et al. (2015): spores germinating after BAC exposure explain reduced effectiveness
disagreements.support: Argues by reasoning that germinated cells should still be killed, so the effect must come from DIC produced at germination or from limited BAC persistence.
disagreements.quote: However, although the spores survive BAC exposure, the germinated microorganisms should be [...] .

disagreements.target: Filtration recommended as a preservation method (Wilson et al. 2020; Mos et al. 2021)
disagreements.support: Cites the authors' earlier work showing filtration alone can fail, and proposes BAC plus filtration.
disagreements.quote: but filtration alone may also not be sufficient to prevent biological changes

disagreements.target: Refrigeration as an effective long-used preservation method (Ascough et al. 2010)
disagreements.support: Cites the authors' earlier finding that DIC, d13C and 14C vary despite refrigeration.
disagreements.quote: Moreover, DIC concentrations, δ13C, and 14C concentrations in natural waters sometimes vary despite refrigeration

alternatives_considered.alternatives: HgCl2, refrigeration, filtration, acid-mediated CO2 extraction in vials, copper or other metal additives
alternatives_considered.reason: Mercury toxicity; refrigeration impossible in some field areas; filters clog with suspended material; vial extraction is too small for 14C; metals alter speciation and isotopes

alternatives_considered.chosen: 14C mass balance with BE to derive DICorg
alternatives_considered.alternatives: DICafter from CO2 quantification at extraction
alternatives_considered.reason: CO2 extraction has uncertainty and cannot be verified

alternatives_considered.chosen: BE averaged from both the DIC-concentration method (Eq. 1) and the d13C isotopic mass balance (Eq. 4)
alternatives_considered.reason: none given; the d13C approach clearly shows the added DIC derives from sugar

alternatives_considered.chosen: Negative or near-zero DICorg replaced by its propagated error
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Using the measured negative value (e.g., -1.0 ± 0.6 mg/L)
alternatives_considered.reason: DICorg must be greater than zero to calculate BE

alternatives_considered.chosen: 2 g/L beet sugar for the BAC experiments
alternatives_considered.reason: Sufficient carbon; the appropriate amount is hard to determine because it depends on the preservation period
